subject: maths
title: Chapter 5 · Test 1
summary: A 25-minute test on Chapter 5 · Decimals: place value, rounding, the four operations with decimals, and terminating and recurring decimals.
body:
This test covers all of Chapter 5 · Decimals: place value in decimals, rounding decimals, adding and subtracting decimals, multiplying and dividing decimals, and terminating and recurring decimals.

## How to do this test

- Allow about 25 minutes.
- No notes and no calculator unless the question says.
- There are 15 questions: 4 easy, 5 medium, 4 hard and 2 challenge.
- Line up decimal points, count decimal places, and estimate to check your answers make sense.
- When you finish, read the worked steps for any question you got wrong, then go back to that lesson.

questions.prompt: What is the value of the digit 4 in 7.148?
questions.explanation: The 4 is the second digit after the point, which is the hundredths place, so it is worth 0.04. Answering 0.4 treats it as tenths, but the tenths digit is 1.
steps: Name the places after the point: 1 is tenths, 4 is hundredths, 8 is thousandths — the places start at tenths.
A digit in the hundredths place is worth that many hundredths: 4 hundredths = 0.04.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the question asks for the value of the digit, not the digit itself. Work out what its place is worth.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the first place after the point is tenths, and the 4 is in the second place. Count the places again.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the 4 is not in the last place. Count the places after the point from the left: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

questions.explanation: The tenths digit is 2 and the next digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so the 2 rounds up to 3: 5.3. Writing 5.2 just chops off the 6 instead of rounding.
steps: 1 decimal place means keep the tenths digit, which is 2 — that is the rounding digit.
The deciding digit is the next one to the right: 6.
6 is 5 or more, so round up: the 2 becomes 3, giving 5.3.

mistakes.A: Step 3: you just cut off the 6. A deciding digit of 5 or more means the rounding digit goes up by 1.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 1 decimal place means you keep the tenths digit — you rounded to a whole number instead.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the 6 is the deciding digit and gets dropped. It is the tenths digit (2) that may change.

questions.explanation: Writing 5.3 as 5.30 and lining up the points gives 5.30 + 2.45 = 7.75. Answering 7.48 adds 3 and 45 as if they were the same kind of part, but 3 tenths is 30 hundredths.
steps: Line up the decimal points and write 5.3 as 5.30 — so both numbers have two decimal places.
Add each column from the right: hundredths 0 + 5 = 5, tenths 3 + 4 = 7, ones 5 + 2 = 7.
Bring the point straight down: 7.75. Check: estimate 5 + 2.5 = 7.5, which is close ✓

mistakes.B: Step 1: you lined up the right-hand ends, so the 5 ones sat in the tenths column. Line up the decimal points instead.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you added 3 + 45 as whole numbers. Write 5.3 as 5.30 so you add 30 hundredths, not 3.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 3 tenths + 4 tenths is only 7 tenths, so nothing carries into the ones column.

questions.explanation: 8 × 6 = 48, and there is one decimal place in 0.8, so the answer is 4.8. Answering 0.48 counts two decimal places, but 6 is a whole number with none.
steps: Ignore the point and multiply: 8 × 6 = 48.
Count decimal places: 0.8 has 1 and 6 has 0, so 1 altogether.
Give the answer 1 decimal place: 48 becomes 4.8. Check: 0.8 is a bit less than 1, so the answer should be a bit less than 6 ✓

mistakes.A: Step 3: 0.8 has one decimal place, so the answer needs one decimal place too. Put the point back in.
mistakes.B: Step 2: only 0.8 has a decimal place — 6 has none — so the answer has 1 decimal place, not 2.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the sign is × (multiply), but you added 0.8 and 6. Multiply the digits instead.

questions.prompt: Put 0.6, 0.06, 0.66 and 0.606 in order from smallest to largest.
questions.explanation: Writing them all with 3 decimal places gives 0.600, 0.060, 0.660 and 0.606, so the order is 0.06, 0.6, 0.606, 0.66. Putting 0.606 last treats it as bigger because it is longer, but 0.660 is bigger than 0.606.
steps: Fill with zeros so each has 3 decimal places: 0.600, 0.060, 0.660, 0.606 — so the columns line up.
Compare tenths first: 0.060 has 0 tenths, so it is smallest. The other three all have 6 tenths.
Compare hundredths: 0.600 and 0.606 have 0 hundredths, 0.660 has 6, so 0.66 is largest; then thousandths: 0.600 is less than 0.606.

mistakes.B: Step 1: you ordered them by how many digits they have. More digits does not mean bigger — fill with zeros and compare place by place.
mistakes.C: Step 3: this list goes from largest to smallest. The question asks for smallest first.
mistakes.D: Step 3: you compared 66 and 606 like whole numbers. Write 0.66 as 0.660, then compare the hundredths digits.

questions.explanation: The hundredths digit is 4 and the next digit is 8, so the 4 rounds up to 5: 3.05. Answering 3.04 forgets to look at the deciding digit.
steps: 2 decimal places means the hundredths digit is the rounding digit: it is 4.
The deciding digit is the next one to the right: 8.
8 is 5 or more, so round up: the 4 becomes 5 and the rest is dropped, giving 3.05.

mistakes.A: Step 3: you dropped the digits after the 4 without rounding. The deciding digit is 8, so the 4 must go up.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you rounded to 1 decimal place. 2 decimal places means keep the tenths AND the hundredths.
mistakes.D: Step 1: you kept 3 digits after the point. 2 decimal places means stop at the hundredths digit.

questions.explanation: Writing 10 as 10.00 and borrowing gives 9 ones, 9 tenths and 10 hundredths, so 10.00 − 4.37 = 5.63. Answering 6.37 only subtracts the whole numbers. Check: 5.63 + 4.37 = 10 ✓
steps: Write 10 as 10.00 and line up the points — so there are tenths and hundredths to subtract from.
Borrow: 10 ones become 9 ones, 9 tenths and 10 hundredths.
Subtract each column: hundredths 10 − 7 = 3, tenths 9 − 3 = 6, ones 9 − 4 = 5, giving 5.63.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you worked out 10 − 4 = 6 and copied the .37. Write 10 as 10.00 and subtract every column.
mistakes.B: Step 2: borrowing takes 1 from the ones, so 10 ones become 9 ones. You left it as 10.
mistakes.C: Step 2: after borrowing for the hundredths, the tenths column should have 9, not 10. Take 1 off it before you subtract.

questions.explanation: 15 × 4 = 60, and there are 2 decimal places in total, so the answer is 0.60 = 0.6. Answering 0.06 throws away the zero in 60 before placing the point.
steps: Ignore the points and multiply: 15 × 4 = 60.
Count decimal places: 1.5 has 1 and 0.4 has 1, so 2 altogether.
Give 60 two decimal places: 0.60, which is 0.6. Check: 1.5 × 0.4 should be less than 1.5 because 0.4 is less than 1 ✓

mistakes.A: Step 2: you counted the decimal places in only one number. 1.5 and 0.4 each have one, so the answer needs 2.
mistakes.B: Step 3: you multiplied 15 × 4 but never put the decimal point back. Count the decimal places in both numbers.
mistakes.D: Step 3: you dropped the zero from 60 before placing the point. Put 2 decimal places into 60 first, then remove the end zero.

questions.explanation: 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875, and the division stops because the remainder becomes 0. Answering 0.78 just writes the digits 7 and 8 after a point.
steps: The fraction bar means divide: 7 ÷ 8. Write 7 as 7.000.
70 ÷ 8 = 8 remainder 6 — write 8 in the tenths.
60 ÷ 8 = 7 remainder 4 — write 7 in the hundredths.
40 ÷ 8 = 5 remainder 0 — write 5 in the thousandths and stop: 7/8 = 0.875.

mistakes.B: Step 1: a fraction is not its digits joined by a point. The fraction bar means 7 ÷ 8.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you worked out 8 ÷ 7. The top number is divided by the bottom number, so divide 7 by 8.
mistakes.D: Step 4: you stopped while there was still a remainder. Keep dividing until the remainder is 0.

questions.explanation: The tenths digit 9 rounds up because the next digit is 6. 9 tenths + 1 tenth = 1 whole, so 19 becomes 20 and the answer is 20.0. Writing 19.10 forgets to carry.
steps: 1 decimal place: the rounding digit is the tenths digit, 9.
The deciding digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so round up.
9 tenths + 1 tenth = 10 tenths = 1 whole, so carry: 19 becomes 20 and the tenths digit becomes 0, giving 20.0 (keep the 0 to show 1 decimal place).

mistakes.A: Step 3: the deciding digit is 6, so the tenths digit must go up, not stay the same.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 9 tenths + 1 tenth = 10 tenths, which is 1 whole. Carry the 1 into the ones instead of writing 10.
mistakes.D: Step 1: you rounded to 2 decimal places. 1 decimal place means keep only the tenths digit.

questions.prompt: Jia buys 1.25 kg of grapes, 0.6 kg of cherries and 2.4 kg of apples. Her bag can hold 5 kg. How many more kilograms could the bag hold?
questions.explanation: The fruit weighs 1.25 + 0.60 + 2.40 = 4.25 kg, and 5.00 − 4.25 = 0.75 kg. Answering 4.25 kg stops before the subtraction.
steps: Add the masses with the points lined up: 1.25 + 0.60 + 2.40 = 4.25 kg.
Subtract from 5: write 5 as 5.00 and borrow — 4 ones, 9 tenths, 10 hundredths.
Hundredths 10 − 5 = 5, tenths 9 − 2 = 7, ones 4 − 4 = 0, so she has room for 0.75 kg more. Check: 4.25 + 0.75 = 5 ✓

mistakes.A: Step 1: you lined up the right-hand ends, so 0.6 was added as 0.06. Line up the decimal points (0.6 = 0.60).
mistakes.C: Step 2: 4.25 kg is what she has already bought. Subtract it from 5 kg to find the space left.
mistakes.D: Step 2: in 5.00 − 4.25 you subtracted the ones and copied the .25. Borrow so you can subtract the tenths and hundredths too.

questions.diagram_alt: Bar model: a whole bar of 5 kg above a bar split into 1.25 kg, 0.6 kg, 2.4 kg and a dashed part labelled ?

questions.explanation: Multiplying both numbers by 100 gives 480 ÷ 6 = 80. Answering 0.8 only changes the divisor, which changes the answer. Check: 80 × 0.06 = 4.8 ✓
steps: The divisor 0.06 has 2 decimal places, so multiply both numbers by 100 — to make the divisor a whole number.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you made 0.06 into 6 but did not change 4.8. Multiply BOTH numbers by the same 100.
mistakes.B: Step 1: you multiplied 4.8 by 10 but 0.06 by 100. Both numbers must be multiplied by the same amount.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 4.8 × 100 is 480, not 4800 — move the point 2 places, not 3.

questions.prompt: Write 11/12 as a decimal using dot notation.
questions.explanation: 11 ÷ 12 = 0.91666…, where only the 6 repeats, so it is written 0.916̇. Putting dots over the 9 and 6 would mean 0.916916…, which is a different number.
steps: Divide 11 by 12: 110 ÷ 12 = 9 remainder 2 — write 9.
20 ÷ 12 = 1 remainder 8 — write 1.
80 ÷ 12 = 6 remainder 8 — write 6. The remainder 8 comes back every time, so the 6 repeats forever.
Only the 6 repeats, so put one dot over the 6: 0.916̇.

mistakes.B: Step 3: dots over the 9 and the 6 mean the whole group 916 repeats. Only the remainder after the 6 keeps coming back, so only the 6 repeats.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you divided 12 by 11. The top number is divided by the bottom: 11 ÷ 12.
mistakes.D: Step 3: the remainder never reaches 0, so the decimal does not stop. Show the repeating digit with a dot.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg bag of rice costs $8.15. What is the price per kilogram, rounded to the nearest cent?
questions.explanation: 8.15 ÷ 3 = 2.71666…, and the digit after the hundredths is 6, so it rounds up to $2.72. $2.71 forgets to round. Check: 3 × 2.72 = 8.16, close to 8.15 ✓
steps: Price per kilogram = cost ÷ kilograms: 8.15 ÷ 3.
Nearest cent means 2 decimal places: the rounding digit is 1 and the deciding digit is 6, so round up to $2.72.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you chopped off the digits after the hundredths. The next digit is 6, so round the cents up.
mistakes.B: Step 1: you multiplied by 3. The price for ONE kilogram is smaller than for 3 kg, so divide.
mistakes.D: Step 1: you divided 3 by 8.15. Divide the cost by the number of kilograms: 8.15 ÷ 3.

questions.prompt: Which of these numbers is the smallest? (The dot means the 3 repeats forever.)
questions.explanation: Written to 3 places the numbers are 0.333…, 0.303, 0.330 and 0.310. All have 3 tenths, and 0.303 has the fewest hundredths (0), so it is smallest. 0.31 looks smaller than 0.303 only if you compare 31 with 303.
steps: All have 3 tenths, so compare hundredths: 0.333… has 3, 0.330 has 3, 0.303 has 0, 0.310 has 1.
0.303 has the smallest hundredths digit, so it is the smallest number.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 0.3̇ is not 0.3 — the dot means 0.333…, which is bigger than all the others here.
mistakes.C: Step 2: compare the hundredths digits: 0.33 has 3 hundredths, more than another option. Write them all with 3 places first.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you compared 31 and 303 like whole numbers. Write 0.31 as 0.310, then compare place by place.
